title: Europe by Night Train: Routes, Costs and How to Book
metaDescription: A practical guide to Europe’s night trains — which routes run, what the cabin classes are really like, how to book, and how they compare to flying.
excerpt: Night trains are back. You board in one capital in the evening and wake up in another, having skipped a hotel night and an airport entirely.
author: Travel Editors
content:
Europe spent two decades dismantling its night train network and has spent the last several rebuilding it. New routes have opened, old ones have been revived, and Austria's ÖBB Nightjet has effectively become the backbone of the continent's sleeper network.

The appeal is straightforward. You board in a city centre in the evening, have dinner, go to sleep, and wake up in another country's city centre. No airport transfer, no security queue, no hotel night. On the right route, it is the best way to travel in Europe.

On the wrong route, it is an uncomfortable night in a shared compartment that costs more than a flight. The difference is knowing which is which.

## The Main Operators

**ÖBB Nightjet (Austria)** runs the largest network, radiating from Vienna and Innsbruck across Germany, Italy, Switzerland, the Netherlands and beyond. The newest rolling stock includes single-occupancy mini-cabins, which have solved the sleeper's biggest problem for solo travellers.

**European Sleeper** operates a Brussels–Amsterdam–Berlin–Prague route, with plans for extensions.

**Snälltåget** runs Sweden to Berlin seasonally.

**Trenitalia and Intercity Notte** cover Italy internally, including Milan and Rome to Sicily — where the train is loaded onto a ferry to cross the strait, which is worth doing for its own sake.

**Caledonian Sleeper** runs London to Scotland, and is excellent.

**Renfe Trenhotel** covers some Spanish and Portuguese routes.

**Various national operators** run domestic sleepers in Poland, Czechia, Hungary, Romania and the Balkans, often very cheaply.

![Rail Travel travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1551294674-a8c8eae64edb?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## The Routes Worth Taking

**Vienna to Venice or Rome** — over the Alps overnight, arriving in Italy for breakfast. One of the best.

**Paris to Vienna** — a long-restored route.

**Brussels or Amsterdam to Vienna and Innsbruck** — the Nightjet spine, useful for reaching the Alps for skiing without flying.

**Berlin to Vienna, Zurich or Paris** — well served, frequent, reliable.

**Zurich to Zagreb or Ljubljana** — a good way into the Balkans.

**Stockholm to Berlin** — seasonal, and a genuinely long journey.

**Rome to Palermo or Syracuse** — the train that boards a ferry.

**London to Fort William** — the Caledonian Sleeper to the Highlands, arriving beneath Ben Nevis. Possibly the single most enjoyable sleeper in Europe.

**Budapest to Bucharest, or Belgrade to Bar** — Eastern European routes that are cheap, slow and scenic. The Belgrade–Bar line through Montenegro is spectacular in daylight, so consider the day service instead.

## The Accommodation Classes, Honestly

This is what determines whether you enjoy it.

**Seats** — the cheapest option and not a good idea for a full night unless you are on a tight budget and young enough not to care. You will not sleep well.

**Couchette (6-berth or 4-berth)** — bunks in a shared compartment, with a sheet and pillow, no privacy, shared with strangers unless you book the whole compartment. The 4-berth is significantly better than the 6. Affordable, sociable, and variable — a good night depends entirely on your compartment-mates.

**Sleeper cabin (1, 2 or 3-berth)** — proper beds, linen, a washbasin in the cabin, sometimes an en-suite shower, and breakfast included. Considerably more expensive and the difference in sleep quality is substantial.

**Mini-cabins** — the newest Nightjet innovation: a private single pod with a bed, a door and a locker. This solves the solo traveller's dilemma of paying for a whole cabin or sharing with strangers, and it is the best value on the network.

**The practical guidance:** if you are travelling as a couple or a small group, book a **private sleeper or a whole couchette compartment**. If you are solo, book a **mini-cabin** where available. A shared 6-berth couchette is the version of night trains that puts people off.

![Rail Travel travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1633886648986-ec392f72d900?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Booking: The Genuinely Annoying Part

Europe's rail booking is fragmented, and night trains are the most fragmented part of it.

- **Book direct with the operator** where possible — ÖBB's site handles most Nightjet routes and is the most reliable
- **Book early.** Sleeper cabins are the first thing to sell out, often months ahead in summer and around holidays. Prices rise steeply as availability drops
- **Tickets typically release three to six months ahead**, varying by operator
- **Rail passes work on some night trains** but always require a supplement for the berth, which is the bulk of the cost. A pass rarely saves much on sleepers
- **Booking sites vary in coverage.** Some aggregators do not show all night train inventory, so check the operator directly before concluding a route does not exist
- **Cross-border routes** are sometimes bookable only through one of the two countries' operators

## What It Actually Costs

A private two-berth sleeper on a major international route typically costs more than a budget flight on the same city pair. The honest comparison, though, includes what you are not paying for:

- A hotel night at the destination
- Two airport transfers
- Checked baggage
- The half-day that flying consumes even on a one-hour flight

Counted that way, a sleeper is frequently cheaper and almost always less tiring. Counted purely on ticket price against a budget carrier, it is not.

## Practical Tips

- **Bring earplugs and an eye mask.** Non-negotiable. Trains are noisy and compartment lights get switched on
- **Bring your own food and water** for the evening. Catering is limited or absent on many services, and station shops close
- **Keep valuables in bed with you.** Theft is uncommon but compartments are accessible, and sleeper cabins lock properly while couchettes vary
- **The attendant usually takes your ticket and passport** overnight so you are not woken at borders. This is normal
- **Showers**, where available, are in the sleeper cars only and there is often a queue in the morning
- **Arrive at the station 20 minutes early**, not an hour. That is the entire point
- **Check the arrival time.** Some services arrive uncomfortably early — 6am in a city where nothing is open, with a hotel that will not check you in until three

## Are They Worth It?

For the right journey, genuinely yes. The best case is an 800 to 1,200-kilometre route between two city centres, on a route where the alternative is a full day of travel or a flight plus two transfers.

The worst case is a short route where the train arrives at 5:30am, or a full 6-berth couchette on a hot summer night.

Choose the route and the cabin class deliberately and the night train is the most civilised way to cross Europe. Book the cheapest option on the longest route and you will arrive wrecked and wondering what the appeal was.

For group trips, the sleeper has one underrated advantage: booking a whole compartment gives you a private space for six, which is cheaper per person than any hotel in Vienna or Zurich, and it removes an entire day of travel from the itinerary. It is worth checking against the flight before assuming flying is simpler — laying both options into the plan with the real door-to-door times usually makes the answer obvious.
